title: Hormuz Talks Hit Snag as Iran Demands Concessions, US Jobs Market Shrinks, Colombia Joins Trump Security Bloc
subhead: Oman-mediated Strait of Hormuz negotiations falter as Iran ties reopening to US concessions and hits an Emirati tanker. The US unexpectedly shed 23,000 jobs. Colombia's new right-wing president immediately aligns with Washington, while the Mecca defence pact reshapes Gulf security.

sections.heading: Hormuz Talks Stall as Iran Sets Conditions and Strikes UAE Tanker
sections.body:
Oman's foreign ministry reported positive talks on securing a shipping route through the Strait of Hormuz on Saturday, but the gaps between the two sides remain wide. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said negotiations were in their final stages but warned that reopening the strait was subject to other conditions — including US compensation for what Tehran calls violations of the June ceasefire memorandum and the lifting of the American naval blockade on Iranian ports.

Iranian security chief Mohammad Baqer Zolqadr told Tasnim that Hormuz would stay closed until the US meets six Iranian demands, including a halt to threats, removal of the port blockade, and release of frozen assets. Vice-President JD Vance, speaking to Fox News, struck a cautious note, saying the US was applying diplomatic, economic and military tools but that the situation was not resolved. Vance also claimed Iran had told Washington it had no plans to toll the strait, contradicting earlier reports that Tehran sought 5-7% cargo fees.

Meanwhile, the UAE said Iran targeted an Adnoc-affiliated tanker with a missile as it transited the strait — a reminder that even as diplomacy advances, military pressure continues. The UK Maritime Trade Operations agency separately reported a ship struck by an unknown projectile off Oman. BBC and Reuters report both incidents.
sections.whyItMatters: The Hormuz impasse is not just about shipping — it is about whether the US-Iran conflict can be de-escalated at all. Iran is linking reopening to war-ending concessions, while the UAE tanker strike shows the risk of miscalculation even during talks.

sections.heading: US Economy Sheds 23,000 Jobs as Labor Market Sours
sections.body:
US employers unexpectedly cut 23,000 jobs in July, a sharp reversal from expectations of roughly 100,000 new positions, according to the Labor Department. Revisions also shaved 103,000 jobs off May and June payrolls. The unemployment rate fell to 4.1%, but only because 264,000 people left the labour force entirely — pushing the participation rate to 61.4%, the lowest since February 2021.

Public schools cut 50,000 positions, restaurants and bars shed 26,000, and retailers eliminated 19,000. The data is a political setback for President Trump less than three months before midterm elections. AP reports that the figures add to pressure from the Iran conflict's economic ripple effects, including the Strait of Hormuz disruption squeezing energy markets.
sections.whyItMatters: A shrinking labour market with falling participation is a warning signal. Combined with energy disruption from the Hormuz closure, the US economy faces compounding headwinds heading into the midterms.

sections.heading: Colombia's New President Takes Office, Joins US Security Pact
sections.body:
Abelardo de la Espriella was sworn in as Colombia's president on Friday and immediately announced Colombia would join the Shield of the Americas security partnership founded by Trump. The US State Department pledged a $1bn security package, calling it a shared effort against organised crime and illegal immigration. De la Espriella, a US citizen since 2023 and self-styled 'El Tigre', used his maiden speech to promise 'all-out war' on drug cartels and armed insurgents.

The move marks a sharp break from his predecessor Gustavo Petro's 'total peace' negotiation approach. De la Espriella also promised a strong military alliance with the US and Israel, reversing Petro's diplomatic break with Israel over Gaza. BBC reports the inauguration continues a broader Latin American shift rightwards amid economic hardship and gang violence.
sections.whyItMatters: A billion-dollar security package and a formal alignment with Trump's security bloc reshapes the western hemisphere's political map. Colombia is now on a collision course with Venezuela and shifts the regional balance toward Washington.

sections.heading: Spain-Italy Schengen Row Escalates as Both Sides Impose Border Checks
sections.body:
Spain imposed border controls on all air and sea travel from Italy at midnight Friday, matching Italy's own suspension of Schengen for arrivals from Spain that began last week. Both countries say the checks will last one month. The dispute stems from the arrival of roughly 78,000 migrants in Spain's Ceuta exclave from Morocco — approximately 100 of whom are believed to have died during the crossing. Nearly 1,400 unaccompanied minors remain in Ceuta.

Italy's Giorgia Meloni says the checks prevent migrants from transiting to Italy; Spain's Pedro Sanchez calls Italy's position based on 'spurious arguments', noting the Ceuta arrivals have no access to the Schengen area. The Czech Republic called for Spain's Schengen membership to be temporarily suspended, while Finland and Denmark backed Italy. BBC Arabic has found dozens of Facebook posts calling for a second crossing in mid-August.
sections.whyItMatters: Two EU members imposing reciprocal border checks is unprecedented. The Ceuta crisis is exposing the fault lines in Europe's migration system and the Schengen agreement itself.

sections.heading: Russia Kills Child Near Kyiv as Zelensky Pleads for Patriots; Serbia Visit Signals New Ties
sections.body:
A child was among three people killed in overnight Russian ballistic missile strikes east of Kyiv, according to regional officials. The attack comes days after 21 were killed in intensified Russian strikes and as President Zelensky warned that Ukraine's supply of Western interceptor missiles has been significantly reduced. Zelensky again called for more US-made Patriot interceptors, noting Ukraine can never match Russian military spending. Trump appeared to walk back a promised Patriot manufacturing licence for Ukraine.

Meanwhile, Zelensky made his first visit to Serbia, meeting President Vučić in Belgrade. The two leaders pledged to finalise a long-stalled free trade agreement by year's end, and Serbia committed 2 million euros for Ukraine's energy sector. Serbia continues to refuse sanctions on Russia but is replacing Soviet-era MiG-29s with French Rafales — a quiet shift away from Moscow. Al Jazeera and BBC report both stories.
sections.whyItMatters: Ukraine's air defence is eroding at a critical moment, and US support is wavering. Serbia's outreach, while symbolically important, does not alter the fundamental imbalance on the battlefield.

sections.heading: Around the World: Mecca Pact Details Emerge, Typhoon Dolphin, Thai Gun Reform
sections.body:
Analysis of the Saudi-Pakistan-Turkey Mecca defence pact, signed Friday, shows it is more strategic signal than operational alliance. Analysts note the mutual-defence clause does not name Iran explicitly, but all three signatories understand it is aimed at containing Tehran and its proxy network. Turkiye brings NATO-standard defence industry, Pakistan brings nuclear weight, and Saudi Arabia brings capital. Iran dismissed the pact through a parliamentary spokesman, saying 'a paper agreement' would not bring security. Al Jazeera reports Kuwait and Qatar may join next.

Typhoon Dolphin battered Japan's Okinawa with 162km/h winds, cutting power to 44,000 buildings and injuring five. China's Zhejiang province raised coastal alerts to the highest level ahead of expected landfall late Sunday. BC Wildfire Service reports a fast-moving wildfire near Summerland, British Columbia has doubled to 36 square miles, forcing over 20,000 evacuations. And in Thailand, Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul pledged to restrict firearms in public to government officials on duty only, after a 14-year-old killed eight people including his grandparents and teachers at a school near Bangkok.
sections.whyItMatters: The Mecca pact's real impact will take years to materialise, but it signals a Gulf states willingness to build security structures outside the US umbrella. The Thai gun reform and BC wildfire response are domestic events with potential regional ripple effects.

bottomLine: The Strait of Hormuz remains closed despite progress in Omani-mediated talks, because Iran is demanding war-ending concessions from the US that Washington has not agreed to — and a missile strike on a UAE tanker shows the strait is still a war zone. The US economy unexpectedly shed jobs, compounding political pressure ahead of midterms. Colombia's new right-wing president immediately aligned with Trump's security bloc, reshaping Latin American alignments. And the Spain-Italy Schengen dispute is stress-testing Europe's open-border system in real time.
